title: Preston Indian Restaurant Faces Licence Loss After Immigration Raid Findings
excerpt: The Silk Route's alcohol licence is under review on October 29 after officers found three staff working outside their visa conditions; the restaurant disputes a £40,000 penalty
body:
• Preston City Council's licensing subcommittee will decide on Thursday, October 29 whether to revoke the alcohol licence of The Silk Route, at West Strand, after the Home Office asked for revocation.
  • Home Office officers who visited in June 2025 found three people working in roles their Skilled Worker and Health and Care visas did not permit; a civil penalty first set at £90,000 has been replaced with £40,000 and is under challenge.
  • The restaurant, through Maya Solicitors, says it was never notified of the original fine, could not appeal in time, and argues the review should wait until its appeal against the findings is decided.
  • For UK employers: GOV.UK states a civil penalty can reach £60,000 per illegal worker, a liable employer has 28 days to respond to a civil penalty notice, and no penalty is due if the employer made the correct right to work checks.

An Indian restaurant in Preston could lose its alcohol licence after a Home Office immigration visit found three people working in jobs their visas did not allow, with Preston City Council's licensing subcommittee set to decide the case on Thursday, October 29.

The Silk Route, at West Strand, was visited by Home Office officials in June 2025. The Home Office is now asking the council to revoke the restaurant's licence, stating its belief that the management is not upholding its duty of preventing crime. Blog Preston reported the details from the submissions made to the council by both sides.

What officers say they found

Officers found a woman working as a waitress and two men in the kitchen. All three held valid Skilled Worker visas, but those visas did not include this type of employment, according to the Home Office submission. The first man said he was helping out in exchange for free food; his visa related to care work, and he admitted he had never worked for his sponsor. The second man initially claimed he had just started and was on leave from his Health and Care Worker sponsor, but later admitted he had worked full-time at the restaurant for a year.

https://x.com/blogpreston/status/2114990734218493982

The manager, Mohammed Ali Enayet, said he had checked the woman's documents but did not realise they specified she had to work in specified fields.

After the visit, the Home Office issued a £90,000 civil penalty. In its original submission to the council it said the fine remained unpaid. The penalty was later revoked and replaced with a £40,000 penalty. The Home Office argues the evidence from the visit is unchanged, and that the change in the penalty should not affect the subcommittee's approach to the licence review.

The restaurant's response

The restaurant says it was never notified of the original fine and was therefore unable to appeal within the allowed six months. In a submission through Maya Solicitors, it argues that a penalty which had never been properly issued should not be taken into consideration during the licensing review. It says the owner is appealing the officers' findings, and that it would only be fair to wait for the conclusion of that appeal before completing the review.

The two positions before the subcommittee are therefore opposed on both fact and process: the Home Office says the June 2025 findings stand and justify revocation, while the restaurant says the penalty process was defective, its challenge is live, and a decision now would pre-judge that challenge.

The rules employers work under

The case sits within the civil penalty regime for illegal working. GOV.UK guidance states that an employer who employs someone without the right to work, without doing the correct checks or doing them properly, can face a civil penalty of up to £60,000 for each illegal worker, with 28 days to respond to a civil penalty notice. It also states that an employer will not have to pay the penalty if it can show it made the correct right to work checks, and that employing someone the employer knew, or had reasonable cause to believe, had no right to work can lead to up to five years in jail and an unlimited fine. A worker holding a valid visa is not automatically permitted to do any job: as this case turns on, visa conditions can restrict the holder to specified employment with a specified sponsor.

Licence review is a separate track from the penalty: the subcommittee can revoke the licence, suspend it, or impose conditions on the evidence before it.

What happens next

The subcommittee meets on Thursday, October 29, with the Home Office seeking revocation and the restaurant asking it to wait for its appeal. Whatever it decides on the licence, the £40,000 penalty remains subject to the restaurant's separate challenge.
